b: Ti West’s Ebenezer tells the tale of a man who, after years of public scorn, seizes on the spirit of Christmas to rehabilitate his image. Go figure, then, that he’s played by Johnny Depp, who, nearly a decade removed from his last role in a major American production, has signed on to this adaptation of A Christmas Carol in a transparent bid for a comeback.

Deviating little from Charles Dickens’s 1843 novella, West’s film follows the miserly moneylender Ebenezer Scrooge through a single Christmas Eve, as he’s visited by the ghosts of Christmas Past, Present, and Future. In what amounts to a Victorian edition of Scared Straight!, the spirits show him the roots of his greed, the toll his cruelty takes on those around him, and the lonely death that awaits him if he doesn’t change his ways.

It’s hard to see what stake anyone besides Depp had in this project beyond cashing in on yet another iteration of A Christmas Carol. Coming off his X trilogy, West is all but anonymous here, trading his gift for grimy, lo-fi horror pastiche for stock Victorian imagery. His 19th-century London is lifeless well before any ghosts show up, and the dialogue scenes—stiffly blocked and chopped up by rapid cutting—undermine any sincere attempt to evoke the period.

Compounding this is the tonal confusion, as the film tries to split the difference between a genuinely macabre ghost story and a family-friendly lampoon of gothic horror. Ebenezer’s few real attempts at fright, such as the Guillermo del Toro-lite prosthetics of the Ghost of Christmas Past (Andrea Riseborough), are undercut by Scrooge’s bathetic wincing at every absurdity the story throws his way, which Depp plays like Saturday-morning slapstick.

The film isn’t incompetent, just unimaginative, and its fidelity to Dickens feels less like an artistic choice than a crutch. Tyler Bates’s score consists largely of somber arrangements of Christmas carols, and the story trudges from one “stave,” or chapter, to the next, each dutifully announced by a title card. Ironically, the film’s lone bold move, renaming the story Ebenezer, abandons the very conceit those touches preserve: Dickens conceived his novella as a carol.

The real purpose of the title change, it seems, is to foreground the humanity of a man shunned by society and in search of redemption—his misdeeds not an obstacle to that redemption but an essential part of it. That framing conveniently doubles as Depp’s own pitch. As he rehashes the eccentric tics that have defined his performances across his career, he’s banking on audiences forgetting the public turmoil that’s consumed his life over the past several years and remembering only the Jack Sparrows and Willy Wonkas. There’s a palpable desperation to his phoned-in whimsy, and it grows more dispiriting the longer Ebenezer sputters on. Watching him writhe, moan, and mug is like listening to a talking doll whose batteries are dying.

Of course, a film’s PR aspirations should be weighed separately from the work itself, but that’s hard to do when Ebenezer shows so little spark or artistic purpose of its own. It has no gimmick to speak of, like the Muppets or the ghoulish motion capture of Robert Zemeckis’s A Christmas Carol, nor does it reshape the story in any meaningful way. Depp’s presence is its sole raison d’être, which is precisely why the whole endeavor feels so cynical.
